title: Security Groups
explanation:
Security groups act as virtual firewalls for your AWS resources, controlling inbound and outbound traffic at the Elastic Network Interface (ENI) level. They are **stateful** — if you allow an inbound request, the response traffic is automatically allowed regardless of outbound rules, and vice versa.

Security groups operate on an allow-only model. You can specify rules that permit traffic, but you cannot create explicit deny rules. Any traffic not explicitly allowed is implicitly denied. This is a fundamental difference from Network ACLs, which support both allow and deny rules.

Key characteristics:
- **Stateful**: Return traffic is automatically allowed. If you allow inbound TCP/443, the response flows out without needing an outbound rule for that connection
- **ENI-level**: Security groups attach to network interfaces, not subnets. Multiple instances in the same subnet can have different security groups
- **Self-referencing**: A security group can reference itself or other security groups as a source/destination, enabling dynamic rules that adapt as instances scale
- **Multiple groups**: Up to 5 security groups can be assigned to a single ENI (configurable up to 16). Rules from all groups are aggregated
- **Default behavior**: New security groups allow all outbound traffic and deny all inbound traffic

For the SAP-C02 exam, security groups are tested in layered security designs (defense in depth with NACLs), self-referencing patterns for auto-scaling groups, and cross-VPC security group references in peered VPCs. Understanding the stateful nature and how it differs from NACLs is a frequent exam topic.
analogy: Security groups are like a VIP guest list at a private event. The bouncer (security group) checks if you are on the list (allow rule) before letting you in. Once you are inside, you can leave freely (stateful — return traffic allowed). If you are not on the list, you are turned away (implicit deny). The bouncer never has a 'banned' list — they only have an 'allowed' list. And each room (ENI) can have its own bouncer with a different guest list.
keyPoints: Security groups are stateful — return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted without explicit rules
Only allow rules are supported; there are no deny rules. Traffic not matching any allow rule is implicitly denied
Security groups operate at the ENI (network interface) level, not the subnet level — different instances in the same subnet can have different groups
A security group can reference another security group as a source or destination, enabling dynamic scaling without IP-based rules
Up to 5 security groups per ENI by default (increasable to 16), with rules aggregated across all attached groups
Changes to security group rules take effect immediately — no need to restart instances or connections
Default security group allows all inbound from itself and all outbound; custom security groups deny all inbound and allow all outbound

examKeywords.definition: A stateful virtual firewall at the ENI level that uses allow-only rules to control inbound and outbound traffic. Return traffic is automatically permitted.
A firewall that tracks connection state. If inbound traffic is allowed, the corresponding outbound response is automatically allowed without a separate rule.
A security group rule that references itself or another security group as the source, allowing all members of that group to communicate — ideal for auto-scaling.
Elastic Network Interface — a virtual network card attached to an instance. Security groups are applied at the ENI level, not the instance or subnet level.

commonMistakes: Confusing security groups (stateful, ENI-level, allow-only) with NACLs (stateless, subnet-level, allow and deny)
Not using security group references as sources — hardcoding IP addresses breaks when instances scale or are replaced
Assuming the default security group is empty — it actually allows all inbound traffic from other instances in the same security group
Forgetting that security groups are VPC-scoped — you cannot reference a security group from another VPC unless using VPC peering with the same Region
Opening 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH (port 22) or RDP (port 3389) — this is a critical security anti-pattern flagged by AWS Config and Security Hub
